speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Connectivity is essential to Singapore and our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many Singaporeans rely on public transport for our daily activities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also rely on our air and sea connectivity to bring in essential goods, support the growth of our industries and connect Singaporeans with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are now connected to about 420 cities through almost 120 airlines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As one of the busiest ports in the world, our maritime hub is a key node in global supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our connectivity to the world is critical not just during peacetime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, it was our strong connectivity to the region and beyond that allowed Singapore to receive and send out critical supplies, including food and medical essentials.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Within Singapore, we worked hard to maintain connectivity by keeping our public transport services running, so that our essential workers could continue to go to work to fight the crisis and keep the country going.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: All these benefits cannot be achieved without the safe and reliable provision of essential air, land and sea transport services at all times and under all circumstances, including during a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our objective is to help Singapore prepare for possible extreme scenarios that may happen in future, so that we are ready for these risks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, we cannot rule out the risk of malicious actors gaining control and adversely influencing our key transport entities, jeopardising the provision of essential transport services in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have built strong relationships with the firms in our transport ecosystem and worked closely with them during peace time and crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, to provide safe, reliable and efficient services for Singapore, and we want to make sure that they continue to do so in the years ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are not alone in making moves to safeguard our essential transport services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other countries have taken steps to protect their strategic assets too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the United States (US), the Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernisation Act was passed in 2018 to expand the jurisdiction of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US, to address growing national security concerns over foreign investment in US companies or operations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is essential to our survival as a nation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I am not saying that just because I chair the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Transport.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our air and seaports have maintained long-running reputations as efficient and reliable hubs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I do not think anyone can seriously argue against the need to ensure the resilience of critical firms in the sector as well as the essential services they provide.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as we are not looking to nationalise these private businesses, the real question is how we can safeguard their resilience in a way that does not make us less business-friendly by ensuring comprehensibility, predictability and fairness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the ownership and management controls in this Bill mirrors those that are contained in the SIRA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister explain – and I think Minister had sort of explained to some extent in his opening speech – why the proposed regime in the Bill is necessary; and possibly can he elaborate a bit more why the critical transport sector firms could not have been designated under the SIRA?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Minister also elaborated to some extent in his opening speech but maybe a further elaboration on that would be useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reliable provision of essential transport services must necessarily be in the "interest of Singapore's national security" under the SIRA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, are these sectors specific application of the Critical Firms Bill also being practised in other jurisdictions globally and can MOT share if we are in line with international practices and coverage?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My primary concern with duplicative or overlapping regimes is the potential confusion that businesses and investors would face.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having multiple different regulatory regimes would already drive up investment and compliance costs as the actors will need to figure out their optimal compliance strategy routinely or for any material transaction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should be cautious of the impact on our competitiveness as a business and investment hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When would a specific entity be designated under the general SIRA and when would an entity be designated under an equivalent sectoral regime?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what is the practical difference if one is designated under the latter, as compared to the former?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have not possibly gone through that, because we have not passed this Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But if we do, if there is a situation, it would probably be useful to know.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially since we have already set up the Office of Significant Investments Review, or OSIR, in connection with the SIRA, which will "serve as a dedicated one-stop touchpoint and closely engage all stakeholders to address their concerns and to minimise the impact on them".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, would an entity that is designated, or is soon to be designated, under this Bill be able to approach the OSIR for guidance as well?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that the designation of entities will take place as soon as the later half of this year, if this Bill is passed by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe the authorities will also be engaging with entities to be designated in relation to compliance with the requirements of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, when will the initial list of designated entities be made known?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like the SIRA, this Bill contemplates targeting particular entities as opposed to an entire sector or industry, the lack of clear criteria may give rise to criticisms of arbitrariness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, are there any guidelines on the criteria, for example, by annual turnover or by market share, that will see a company identified as a designated entity?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For companies that are not on the initial list of designated entities, may I ask whether will there be subsidiary legislation setting out clear procedures and timelines leading up to the Minister’s designation of such entity?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As various consequences follow from the designation of an entity, having clear timelines will allow investors and businesses to plan and execute their responses, such as divestment or "off-ramping".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Minister in some ways alluded to that in his opening speech as well, maybe it would be useful to repeat that again.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The definitions of "equity interest" and "controller" that are sought to be introduced mean that it will not only catch transactions of shares in the designated entities, but also transactions of shares and interests of indirect parent entities one or more levels up the chain.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is further complicated by the range of financial instruments that are traded on the market – equity-linked notes or products – could potentially lead to "control" for the purpose of notification and approval thresholds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would there be detailed guidelines on how such "control" is to be determined and how the relevant authorities intend to continually monitor such ownership changes, especially with varied products and instruments traded out in the market, not just regionally but possibly globally as well?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, I believe the Singapore Government continues to hold a "golden share" of Singapore Airlines such that it has the ability to outvote the other shares and exercise corporate control.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In other scenarios, we have been able to effectively direct the actions of certain companies by subjecting them to licensing regulations, as well as contracting conditions for those who rely heavily on Government contracts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also note that the Bill covers not only Singapore-incorporated companies, but foreign companies that carry out activities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such foreign companies may also be subject to mandatory regulation in their home jurisdiction, including requirements on ownership and control.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we foresee a scenario where companies may be subject to conflicting regulatory requirements in their home jurisdiction and under this Bill, if it is passed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the company may be required to remain 50% state-owned in its home jurisdiction, but that may not be in the interests of ensuring the resilience of our critical transport entities and the essential services they provide.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a similar vein, has the Ministry considered whether it would need to exercise its regulatory power to veto the appointment of CEOs, Board Chairmen and even Board members differently where such officers are being appointed by a foreign headquarter or shareholder in a designated entity?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What if this causes a breach of Board appointment rights granted under a shareholders' agreement?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be careful that our legitimate right to safeguard our national interests is not perceived as simply a protectionist move to reserve these appointments in transport firms for Singaporeans or worse, for Government appointees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also heartening to note that we have been, and intend to continue, adopting a consultative approach in designating entities and exercising regulatory powers under this framework.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond these behind-the-scenes engagement, public clarity is also equally important.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Reassuring investors that our system remains transparent, fair and predictable is the best way to keep our doors open for business, while safeguarding our interest in keeping our critical transport entities and essential transport services resilient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill requires approvals for ownership controls and changes, and various notification requirements, for example, change of ownership or whether there are events which materially impede or impair the provision of such services, together with remedial directions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, I have some clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To start off, may I ask the Minister to share what were some of the risks observed in the prospective critical entities that drove the need for this Bill and for the proposed amendments to the sectoral Acts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Government be publishing any guidelines in the subsidiary legislation on how a person is fit and proper as required under the Act, similar to what is envisaged in the recent Significant Investments Review Act, or SIRA?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These conditions include, among other things, the Minister being satisfied that either type of licensee has contravened the conditions of their licence, the licensee is unable to pay its debt, or in the interests of safety, security and continuity of the provision of such services, or in the case of a railway licensee having contravened the conditions of their licence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the Minister could also administer such an order should they view such a decision as being in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Could the Government provide greater clarity on what public interest entails within the context of the current Bill?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is important as it will not only provide greater clarity for the management of the affected companies, it will also provide clarity and transparency to investors of such companies on the circumstances in which the Government can exercise such powers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, the current Bill proposes that the Government be given similar powers over the shareholders and management of designated operating entities and designated entities in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on what would be the difference in the criteria for assessing national security and the public interest in the respective legislations?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Aside from setting out the Minister's prerogative to issue certain orders and directions to designated entities, the Bill also requires designated entities to report certain matters to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under the Bill, designated entities are required to notify authorities of any event that could materially impede their ability to carry out their essential transport services in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Should such a situation arise in future, in the interest of transparency, will the Government be informing the public such events or even irregularities reported and the remedial actions taken?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Government what is the mechanism which will be put in place to ensure that it can carry out any pre-emptive checks on operators who are reluctant to report any such events or irregularities or to ensure timely rectifications.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While legislation would play a crucial role in buttressing the resilience of Singapore's public transport system, the importance of implementing operational measures should not be ignored as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Part 4, section 27D of the Bill allows the Minister to halt a railway licensee from the provision of their services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, in the event that there is no replacement operator willing to take over at short notice, for example, if they perceive such a move as being financially untenable, would LTA be in a position to take over the operation?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In 2016, the then Transport Minister, Mr Khaw Boon Wan, suggested that LTA should enhance their operational and maintenance team to take over operations should the need arise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would the Government clarify whether LTA currently has the capacity to take over as the operator of last resort and, if not, whether there is an actionable plan or a road map towards such an outcome?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given that PSA Corporation and CAG are already directly or indirectly owned by the Government, in respect of these companies, are the proposed controls on ownership and key personnel in this Bill redundant in any way?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does the Government have any plans to divest its stakes in PSA or CAG?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Have those entities been consulted on the designated entity framework and have they provided any feedback on the impact that such designation might have on their operations?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does the Minister anticipate that the designated entity framework may, in any way, affect Changi Airport's attractiveness for investment from companies that may have more efficient and innovative or just different approaches to airport services?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 28 defines essential transport services in the CAAS Act as various services and facilities provided to support the operations at Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Operations at Seletar Airport are thus not deemed to be essential transport services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To what extent will the current players be affected?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, will all the current bunker companies supplying fuel within port limits be included?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What about the companies that supply bunkers also in the outside port limits area?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The provisions in the Bill lack a clearer framework that outlines regulatory processes, procedures, criteria and guidelines to help the Government to regulate or operationalise in accordance with the intentions of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope such details will be included clearly in the subsidiary legislation after the Bill has been passed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Just now, the Minister mentioned about the advisory guidelines and I hope such guidelines will be included in the subsidiary legislation eventually.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is important, lest the lack of such details and transparency may affect investor confidence in the transport sector or in affected companies, particularly the certainty of their investment in the longer run.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, what will be the regulatory or legislative powers granted to personnel involved?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Particularly for maritime and aviation, will there be any impact on Singapore's trade flows?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications, I am seeking the Workers' Party's support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two points of clarifications to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can the Minister clarify how MOT expects this Bill to impact the transport sector in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry consulted with these entities and, if so, can their concerns be shared with this House?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, is MOT concerned that increased regulation and control may affect the growth of our transport sector by slowing down business transactions or increasing barriers for new enterprises?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, startups which intend to grow to become key players in our aviation and maritime ecosystem may face challenges in bringing in new members if there is a risk of greater regulatory controls in the future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or are we expecting that these new safeguards will allow an even more open approach to the transport sector, allowing more private ownership and foreign investment, even for critical areas?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will we invite more overseas transport operators to join our public bus network?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification relates to the interaction of this Bill with the Significant Investments Review Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Member Saktiandi spoke about this and the Minister also spoke about this in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify why separate rules are created in this Bill under four different Acts, rather than being implemented through the framework created under the Significant Investments Review Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, all the entities to be designated under this Bill could have been designated as critical to national security instead and brought under the purview of the Office of Significant Investments Review instead, with MOT being consulted as a subject matter expert.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One such complexity is that under the Significant Investments Review Act, the Minister's decisions can be appealed to a Reviewing Tribunal rather than judicial review under the Courts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, decisions under this Bill would be appealed through the judicial review process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I trust both forums to be capable of reaching fair decisions, the difference in forum might lead to inconsistency in process or outcomes, which may create uncertainty for business owners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There can be no doubt our transportation sector is the lifeblood of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing regional conflicts highlight the importance of ensuring its resilience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While increased controls are critical, it is important to understand how they might impact certain areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I would like to seek some clarifications on the Bill's potential impact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, can we achieve the goal of strengthening security measures, without stifling innovation within these critical firms?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has a strong reputation for being a hub for innovation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We want our transport sector to be at the forefront of pioneering new technologies like autonomous vehicles, green transportation solutions and logistical optimisation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I believe that it is crucial to explore ways to amend this Bill to strike a balance between security and innovation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we create a framework that allows these critical firms to flourish while safeguarding our national interests?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to consider the potential impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes increased Government oversight for critical transport firms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this regime affect the day-to-day operations of these critical firms?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will they face significant disruptions or bureaucratic hurdles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, is there a concern that the additional regulatory burden could discourage foreign investment or hinder the growth of local firms?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises concerns about the intent of Government reach in personnel decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does this hinder a company's ability to function as a truly private entity, considering that even CEO and board appointments require agency approval?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will such overarching Government involvement in the appointment of personnel affect the ability of such companies in attracting talent?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will our companies risk losing talent because of the time lag or the need for approval sought to appoint them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Global and even local talent can easily find appointment in jurisdictions with less red tape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill's agency approval process for acquiring and liquidating shares has potential implications for stock trading of these companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The potential time delays associated with approvals could hinder stock exchange activities and impact profitability, potentially leading to financial losses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to ensure that this Bill does not create unnecessary obstacles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there ways to minimise the burden on businesses while still achieving the desired security outcomes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this Bill affect operations in the bus contracting model in attracting companies to bid as their appointments would come under scrutiny?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government provide a timeline for the approval process for manpower?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, another key concern is the potential impact on competition within the transport sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Increased Government control might inadvertently lead to consolidation, with larger firms potentially absorbing smaller ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While some consolidation might be inevitable, we need to ensure that the Bill does not create an environment where smaller firms struggle to compete under stricter regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thus, it is crucial to explore how the Bill can be structured to ensure a healthy level of competition within the critical transport sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A competitive landscape fosters innovation and keeps costs in check.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We do not want the Bill to inadvertently create monopolies or duopolies that could preclude innovation and, ultimately, raise costs for consumers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will Singaporeans have to pay more for public transportation as a result?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, concerns remain about transparency and the appeal process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While national security is paramount, how will transparency be ensured around these interventions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the process for appealing decisions made by the relevant authorities under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there an independent body that can review Ministerial decisions or decisions by the authorities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, the Bill needs to clearly define the circumstances that will justify the Minister intervening in the operations of a critical transport firm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What specific circumstances would trigger such intervention and how would such Ministerial intervention be carried out in a transparent and accountable manner?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards are in place to prevent the Minister from abusing these powers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the Bill's impact on our global standing needs careful consideration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's position as a major transportation hub cannot be overstated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this Bill affect our attractiveness to foreign investors and our overall standing in the global transport industry?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to ensure that the Bill does not create unnecessary friction with our international trade partners who rely on Singapore's efficient transport system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government assure that the Bill will not unfairly disadvantage foreign companies, compared to local firms?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Maintaining a level playing field is critical for attracting and retaining foreign investment in this vital sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, as we deliberate on this Bill, several key considerations emerge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, we must balance security measures with fostering innovation within these firms, safeguarding our reputation as an innovative hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Amendments to the Bill should aim at nurturing innovation while upholding security imperatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourthly, transparency and an effective appeal process are paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifthly and finally, we must assess the global implications of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's attractiveness to foreign investors and its global standing as a transportation hub should not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In closing, while supporting the Bill, we must address these concerns to strike a balance between security, innovation, business viability, transparency and global competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that the Bill enhances rather than hinders our transport sector's growth and resilience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us work together to strengthen our transport sector without impeding its progress and global competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I refer to the Transport Sector (Critical Firms) Bill and I would like to highlight certain concerns.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One of them applies across all industries, which is, how are we going to be able to attract good talents in leadership roles?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Another is, how do we navigate our strategic business expansion and diversification plans?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For any economy to grow, the transport infrastructure must facilitate the flow of goods and services, and people mobility must be well-connected to businesses around the world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Transport is the key to economic growth and competitiveness for trade.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the words of Mr Gan Kim Yong, our Trade Minister, "Trading is Singapore's lifeline.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But more than just that, it is in Singapore's DNA".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our airport and seaport are the catalysts of our economic development.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Against the backdrop of escalating geopolitical tensions, it is imperative that Singapore takes proactive measures to safeguard the operations of its essential transport services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Transport Sector (Critical Firms) Bill stands as a testament to our unwavering commitment to fortify the resilience and security of our transport networks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Nonetheless, I would like to bring forth a few clarifications and suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Should these pivotal positions be reserved exclusively for Singaporeans, or should Permanent Residents also be considered?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, what stance should we adopt regarding foreigners occupying these critical roles?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What mechanisms would MOT employ to ensure that the Chairmen and the CEOs of such designated equity entities are aligned with the public interest of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How would MOT respond if a designated equity interest holder is not aligned with Singapore's interests?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We are keen to understand how MOT has been preparing for such an eventuality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Will it enlist staff experienced in managing essential transport services to strengthen its bench strength during peace time in preparation for such contingencies?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Will there be sufficient experience personnel and capabilities within MOT ready to step in and fill the gap?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Fourthly, it is worth noting that point-to-point (P2P) platform service providers are currently not regulated under the Transport Sector (Critical Firms) Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Lastly, within large organisations, essential transport services and specific capabilities may reside within specific divisions or departments of the large organisations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How would MOT validate their capabilities and readiness to provide such services in both peacetime and crisis?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would MOT consider mandating this entities as separate companies for better streamlined regulation and administration?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These questions and suggestions are raised to ensure the efficacy and comprehensiveness of the Transport Sector (Critical Firms) Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As we navigate the intricate terrain of our transport landscape, let us remain vigilant and proactive in safeguarding the interests of our nation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I eagerly await the Minister's response to address the above five points.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Doing so will ensure that the sectors will operate under conditions to better support and enhance our national security interests.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, I would like to ask if there was any recent incident in Singapore that have prompted the introduction of this new legislation?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry share the specific risk or vulnerability that is being addressed by this Bill?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on the criteria to be used to determine which entities qualify as "essential" and the implications of this designation?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a small country with an open economy, for decades, we have been welcoming investments in many sectors from foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned about the potential dampening effect on collaboration, innovation and new investments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   During this period of greater international tensions between some nations, particularly between the US and China, how will the MOT manage potential sensitivities and conflicts of interest among designated equity interest holders, especially for the air and sea sectors?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Entities designated under this Bill will not be concurrently designated under Sira.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how these two pieces of legislation work together to avoid areas of overlap or potential conflicts?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My final question is regarding the Ministry's consultation with industry representatives on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry share with the House their concerns and feedback, particularly on its potential impact on businesses and investors, and how these are addressed in the Bill? : I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to put in place safeguards to protect critical transport firms from extreme scenarios in future and ensure the continued resilience of essential transport services in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Wee and Mr Louis Ng asked about the potential overlap between this Bill and SIRA.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SIRA is designed to complement sectoral legislation and safeguards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Where possible, the preference is for sector leads to enforce controls over the entities under their purview, as they are most familiar with their sectors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Wee and Mr Saktiandi asked about the criteria for designation and Mr Ng asked about the number of designated entities under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are various criteria that will be taken into consideration for designation, including whether the entity is involved in the provision of essential transport services, and whether it is strategically important in the sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: An entity may be considered strategically important if it has significant market share or specialised expertise in the industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Designated entities are thus unlikely to be smaller companies with lower market share in the industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Designated entities may include firms owned by the Government or Temasek Holdings, they could also include firms owned by other shareholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked whether we will consider designating P2P operators under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It serves a complementary role to public transport to meet the commuting needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have an on-going review of the P2P industry structure and regulatory framework, and a decision can be taken after the review is completed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked whether Seletar Airport will be covered under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have not included Seletar Airport in the definition of essential transport services in the Bill, as it currently functions as a secondary airport to Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The respective authorities will review the list of designated entities from time to time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They will engage and consult the entities prior to designation, and the notifications of designation will be published in the Gazette at least 14 days before the date that the designation takes effect.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Ang asked whether equity interest holders that are predominant owners of a designated operating entity will be required to seek approval for Chairpersons and CEOs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, we may designate equity interest holders that have a strong nexus of control over the designated operating entity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If designated, these equity interest holders will also need to seek approval for appointment of their Chairpersons and CEOs, to protect the interests of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Ang asked if we will mandate larger entities to restructure and register specific departments that manage essential transport services as separate entities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Wee and Mr Ng asked for more details on our consultation with entities on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have engaged key transport firms on the Bill and the relevant authorities will finalise the list of designated entities after the Act comes into force.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have taken onboard the feedback from the engagements.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, some firms asked for more clarification on the "materiality" threshold for notification.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will prepare guidelines, as I mentioned earlier, to provide greater clarity on the types of events that would require notification.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Wee, Mr Ng, Mr Tan and Ms Poh Li San asked if the Bill's controls could affect the economic competitiveness, innovation or growth of the transport industry, as they felt they might disadvantage foreign companies, discourage new investments, or increase barriers for new enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proposed Bill is about enhancing the resilience of essential transport services in Singapore, by safeguarding strategically important transport firms against adverse influence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will not adversely impact the transport industry or create significant compliance costs and regulatory burden for entities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Neither will it affect the day-to-day operations of the transport firms.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Many of the controls under the Bill are not new and already exist in our sectoral Acts or licence conditions today.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What this Bill seeks to do is to consolidate some of these existing controls under a common legislative framework and extend it to other entities, including some non-licensees.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The existing licensing regimes remain in effect and will continue to regulate standards and performance of the day-to-day operations of our licensed entities to ensure that they continue to operate their services in a safe, reliable and efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi asked how the requirements under our Bill would be deconflicted with overlapping requirements in shareholders’ agreements or the law in the home jurisdiction of foreign-owned entities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Shareholders can continue to appoint Board members as provided for in their agreements, but the relevant appointments will require approval from the Authorities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Each decision for approval will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Authorities will assess the circumstances of each case and try to process the applications as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have also carefully calibrated the controls to impose only what is necessary to achieve our policy objective of safeguarding the provision of essential transport services in Singapore, while ensuring that our transport industry remains open, pro-business and investor-friendly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One example is how we differentiated the controls for designated operating entities and designated equity interest holders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Poh asked about the criteria for assessing changes in ownership and the appointment of key personnel in designated entities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will consider a range of factors before coming to a decision, but the main focus is to protect Singapore's national interests and to safeguard our critical transport firms against adverse influence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will not assess applications based on nationality alone and we are not reserving appointments for any particular nationality or group of persons.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Tan also asked whether the Government will be publishing guidelines on what a "fit and proper" person is, as this is one of the approval criteria for ownership controls.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our approach will take reference from these legislation as far as possible, while taking into account the needs of the respective transport sectors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Poh asked whether ownership controls would apply to the non-transport related business arms of designated entities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it depends on how the entities structure their business operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This Bill does not interfere with the day-to-day operations or private commercial decisions of the critical transport firms.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to protect Singapore and Singaporeans against potential threats to the safety and reliability of our essential transport services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In such scenarios, MOT could use the proposed safeguards in this Bill to prevent undesirable individuals from being appointed to key positions in these firms, or to disallow certain persons from acquiring significant shareholdings.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In response to Mr Yip's question about the possible time delays associated with approvals, the relevant authorities will endeavour to minimise undue delays.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For bona fide applications, the firms should have nothing to worry about, as the applications will be given expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For problematic cases, I think Mr Yip would agree that it is not in Singapore’s interests for the authorities to give quick approvals in such situations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In response to Mr Saktiandi's question, the relevant authorities will monitor ownership changes in designated entities, but it is ultimately the responsibility of those becoming or ceasing to become controllers of a designated entity to ensure that prior approval is obtained or prior notice is given, where applicable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There may be remedial directions and penalties if they fail to do so.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Poh Li San and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the triggers and implementation process for the Special Administration Order.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are questions on when such orders would be issued on the “public interest” grounds, and what this might entail.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Keeping the scope broad will provide us with sufficient flexibility to respond quickly to new risks that may emerge over time, or unexpected scenarios in future.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The order will only be activated as a last resort and in the extreme scenario and unlikely event that a designated entity becomes unable to provide essential transport services safely and reliably.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is similar to the step-in arrangements for critical firms in other sectors, such as power and water.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When an order is issued, the Minister will appoint a person, who may be the respective authorities, operators or other third parties with the requisite competencies, to manage the affairs, business and property of the designated entity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The main objective is to ensure that the entity can continue to provide the essential services and I think it is in such situations, a safe assumption to make, that many of the employees of the entity will still be there, working there, and so we will also be working together with the employees who are there, who are familiar with the operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the key, as I said, is to ensure that the entity can continue to provide the essential services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi asked why the penalties for non-compliance differ across the four Acts and whether the penalties are sufficient to incentivise compliance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In deciding the penalties under this Bill, we took reference from existing penalties under the framework of each of our sectoral Acts, and the different considerations and needs of entities across the transport sectors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The existing penalties have worked well so far in deterring errant behaviour, without imposing excessive burden on bona fide firms.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip Hong Weng asked about the safeguards in place to ensure transparency, as well as the appeal process under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is no appeal provision for the Special Administration Order under our existing Acts, as prompt action is required in such situations to respond quickly and safeguard the continuity of essential transport services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I hope Members understand why, for Special Administration Order, this is a separate process.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is also similar to the approach taken in other sectoral legislation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I agree with Members that it is important to assure investors and businesses, both local businesses and international businesses, that our doors remain open and that our system continues to be transparent and fair.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: All powers under the Bill will be exercised judiciously and in accordance with clearly defined procedures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Can I just clarify with the Minister that he said that the Chairman and the CEO of the designated equity interest holder need approval by MOT?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If so, does it mean that a foreign company, which is a holding company that majority owns a designated operating entity in Singapore, needs approval from MOT, even if the foreign company is a listed company in their home country?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: That means if they are listed and not in Singapore, they also require their Chairman and their group CEO to be approved by MOT?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am not sure the Minister has answered some of my questions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Regarding my question, in a situation where there is no replacement operator willing to take over at short notice under Part 4, section 27DE, I asked whether LTA would be in a position to take over the operation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Currently, what is the position, whether they are able to do so or whether there is an actionable plan or roadmap towards such an outcome?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As to whether this then leads to the point that Mr Tan is making, I think probably a little bit of extrapolation on Mr Tan's part.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This Bill, by itself, does not go anywhere near those further points that Mr Tan is making.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is just to provide the safeguards for our critical transport firms and our essential transport services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because as I mentioned in my response speech earlier, this cannot be done just by LTA alone.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will also have to work closely with, first and foremost, the employees and the staff who are working in the entity who know the operations best.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Many of them will still be there, even if the entity were to run into trouble and we need to issue, in an extreme scenario, a Special Administration Order.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will have to work closely with them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we will need support from the staff, the unions, and also for some of the sectors where there is more than one operator, the expertise from the other operators could also come in to help us.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is not just an LTA alone effort.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But certainly, we will need to make preparations and we will need to get ready to deal with all these different scenarios so that we are well prepared.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Speaker, I thank Minister Chee for his comprehensive reply.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Minister Chee assured us that only as a last resort in extreme scenarios will the step-in powers be exercised.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Given the scale and complexity of our transportation system, how likely is MOT or the agencies able to find replacement leadership with the right capabilities at short notice to lead the designated entities out of trouble, especially since this industry only has a few big players?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For example, SMRT, we know, took quite a few years with all hands on deck to get back to where they were.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: So, I would like the Minister to further clarify this part.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, a lot of the things that we do before that extreme scenario happens is to really help us to mitigate the risks to prevent those risks from turning into an extreme scenario so that we can avoid going to this last resort, if possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we still need to be ready in case those risks were to emerge, those extreme scenarios were to happen in future.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do not want to be caught unprepared.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is why we wanted to have this Bill, to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will use the Special Administration Order as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we really need to do that, yes, it is there, but we would prefer not to go down that path.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We would prefer to use prevention rather than cure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am not sure whether I missed part of his closing speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I actually asked a question about OSIR in connection with SIRA, which serves as a dedicated one-stop touchpoint to engage all stakeholders and address their concerns and minimise the impact on them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But for this Bill, it is very sectoral based.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will MOT actually utilise OSIR to handle stakeholder questions or concerns going forward or will there be a separate sectoral-based entity?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In our case, because we have the sectoral authorities – CAAS, LTA, MPA – they will be the ones who will play the role of this office to deal with the respective firms within their sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The reason for the amendment has been explained in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The reason for the amendment has been explained in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The consequential amendments* to be made, will be made.
